extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians, problem-setters, graduate students, and mathematical educators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for formulating and evaluating mathematical problems (especially research-level) that are clear, suitably difficult, significant, and productive of new methods and further questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and easy comprehensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: "What is clear and easily comprehended attracts, the complicated repels us." The very statement of the problem must be intelligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good problem's statement should be readily understood; obscurity in formulation is a symptom of weakness rather than depth. Avoid vague or jargon-heavy formulations; make the question intelligible to a mathematically educated reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate difficulty (difficult but accessible)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Difficult in order to entice us, yet not completely inaccessible, lest it mock at our efforts." The problem should lie at the edge of current capability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose problems that are challenging enough to motivate effort and develop new ideas, but not so hard that no approach is available. Too easy problems are uninteresting; too hard problems may be barren.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance (advances mathematical science)
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem must matter — its solution should move mathematics forward rather than merely add another datum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate problems by their potential gain to science: will solving it resolve important issues, clarify foundational matters, or have broad impact? Prefer problems whose solutions influence subsequent development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lay-comprehensibility of the result ("first man on the street" standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: "A mathematical theory is not to be considered complete until you can explain it to the first man whom you meet on the street." Completeness includes the ability to explain results to a non-specialist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for results and statements that can be conveyed intelligibly to an educated non-specialist; if the theorem requires excessive expert vocabulary to state, the theory may be unfinished. This emphasizes clear exposition and conceptual clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vitality of a field measured by abundance of problems
rubrics_metrics.description: "As long as a branch of science offers an abundance of problems, so long is it alive; a lack of problems foreshadows extinction."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge research programs partly by whether they generate further problems. A healthy field produces many open questions; a field with few problems risks stagnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value judged by methods developed
rubrics_metrics.description: The final award depends upon the gain which science obtains from the problem — in particular the methods developed pursuing its solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize problems whose pursuit yields new techniques and perspectives. A solution that requires genuinely new methods is more valuable than one solved by existing routine techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational reach
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems often have foundational scope (e.g., consistency of arithmetic, axiomatization), affecting core aspects of a subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems that bear on foundations or basic principles are especially important because their resolution can reshape large areas of mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer general statements rather than isolated specific instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate problems in a way that captures broad phenomena or general principles rather than narrow special cases; generality increases applicability and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection across fields (cross-disciplinary linkage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good problems often link different areas (logic, geometry, number theory, physics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems that connect multiple domains tend to stimulate broader progress and transfer of methods; favor questions that foster interdisciplinary interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concreteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Even foundational problems should be stated as specific questions, not vague programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State problems with concrete, precise formulations and clear success criteria to avoid ambiguity about what counts as a solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational test / definite success criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Each problem should have a definite criterion for when it would be 'solved.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the problem has an operational test or clear answer condition so that progress and success can be unambiguously assessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opens further questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer problems whose solutions open many new questions, rather than those that merely close a case without further consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a result by whether it generates new directions and problems; work that spawns further inquiry is especially valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answerability / determinacy
rubrics_metrics.description: "Wir müssen wissen — wir werden wissen." The normative idea that well-posed mathematical questions should in principle have determinate answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate problems so they are, in principle, resolvable; avoid questions that cannot be settled even in principle, since such problems are poor candidates for productive mathematical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: unclear or obscure statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems whose statement is itself unclear are often a sign of confusion, not depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid opaque formulations. If a problem's meaningful content cannot be explained clearly, reconsider or reformulate it; obscurity is a disqualifying trait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: problems that are too easy
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems that are too easy are uninteresting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not prioritize trivial or routine questions that add little to knowledge or method; seek challenges that require substantive effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: problems that are too hard/inaccessible
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems that are completely inaccessible mock our efforts and may be barren.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid posing problems with no plausible approaches or that lie hopelessly beyond current methods; such problems rarely yield useful progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: solutions that do not advance larger goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems whose solution would not advance any larger goal are of limited value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of problems whose resolution produces only isolated facts without methodological or conceptual impact; favor problems tied to broader aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: technical opacity to the educated public
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories so technically encrusted that they cannot be conveyed to the educated public are problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for conceptual transparency and the ability to communicate results beyond a narrow specialist circle; excessive technical encrustation suggests unfinished exposition or lack of conceptual clarity.
